topic: R2.2 How fast? The rate of chemical change
subject: chemistry

items.q: Hydrogen peroxide decomposes: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). Which quantity is the rate of this reaction at a particular moment?
items.correct: The decrease in the concentration of H₂O₂ per unit time at that moment
items.misconception: The total time taken for all of the H₂O₂ in the sample to decompose
items.why: In practical work students often record 'the time taken' (for a cross to disappear, or for a solid to dissolve) and call it 'the rate', and in everyday speech 'how fast' and 'how long' are used loosely for the same idea. A rate is a quantity divided by a time, with units such as mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ or cm³ s⁻¹. The time taken for a fixed amount of change is inversely related to the average rate: a reaction that takes longer has the smaller rate.
items.specStatementText: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
items.random_wrong: The total volume of O₂ given off by the time the reaction has stopped

items.q: Magnesium ribbon reacts with excess hydrochloric acid, and the hydrogen is collected in a gas syringe. A graph of the volume of hydrogen (y-axis, cm³) against time (x-axis, s) is a curve that is steep at first, becomes less steep and levels off at 60 cm³ at 100 s. The curve passes through the point (20 s, 34 cm³). A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 20 s passes through the points (0 s, 10 cm³) and (40 s, 58 cm³). What is the rate of reaction at t = 20 s?
items.correct: 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹
items.misconception: 1.70 cm³ s⁻¹
items.why:
In a straight-line graph through the origin, y/x equals the gradient, and students carry this shortcut over to curves. It also resembles 'speed = distance/time' learned in physics. For a curve, y/x at a point gives the average rate since the start, not the rate at that instant. The instantaneous rate is the gradient of the tangent: Δy/Δx between two points on the tangent line.

Working: Gradient of the tangent at t = 20 s = Δ(volume)/Δ(time) = (58 cm³ − 10 cm³)/(40 s − 0 s) = 48 cm³/40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
items.random_wrong: 0.60 cm³ s⁻¹
items.working: Gradient of the tangent at t = 20 s = Δ(volume)/Δ(time) = (58 cm³ − 10 cm³)/(40 s − 0 s) = 48 cm³/40 s = 1.20 cm³ s⁻¹.

items.q: The concentration of a reactant, R, is followed at constant temperature. A graph of [R] (y-axis, mol dm⁻³) against time (x-axis, s) is a curve that starts at 0.0500 mol dm⁻³, becomes less steep and reaches zero at 1500 s. The curve passes through the point (300 s, 0.0220 mol dm⁻³). A tangent drawn to the curve at t = 300 s passes through the points (0 s, 0.0370 mol dm⁻³) and (600 s, 0.0070 mol dm⁻³). What is the rate of reaction at t = 300 s?
items.correct: 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.misconception: 3.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.why:
Students often calculate a single average rate in practical work and treat it as 'the rate'; everyday processes are often pictured as running at a steady speed. The rate changes as the reaction proceeds. The total change divided by the total time gives only the average rate over the whole reaction; the rate at a particular time must be found from the tangent at that time.

Working: Gradient of the tangent at t = 300 s = Δ[R]/Δt = (0.0070 − 0.0370) mol dm⁻³/(600 − 0) s = −0.0300 mol dm⁻³/600 s = −5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The rate is quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [R]: rate = 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
items.random_wrong: 7.33 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.working: Gradient of the tangent at t = 300 s = Δ[R]/Δt = (0.0070 − 0.0370) mol dm⁻³/(600 − 0) s = −0.0300 mol dm⁻³/600 s = −5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The rate is quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [R]: rate = 5.00 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

items.q: Sample P is neon gas at 40 °C. Sample Q contains twice as many krypton atoms as P and is at 20 °C. Which statement comparing the kinetic energies of the atoms in the two samples is correct?
items.correct: The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in P is greater than that in Q, but only by about 7%.
items.misconception: The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in P is twice the mean kinetic energy in Q.
items.why: Everyday temperatures are always in °C, and the proportionality 'energy ∝ temperature' is learned without the kelvin condition; the zero of the Celsius scale looks like a true zero. Convert to kelvin (T = θ + 273) before comparing: 40 °C is 313 K and 20 °C is 293 K, so the mean kinetic energy increases by a factor of only 313/293 ≈ 1.07.
items.specStatementText: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
items.random_wrong: The atoms in Q have the greater mean kinetic energy, as krypton atoms are heavier.

items.q: Two reactant molecules in a gas collide with a combined kinetic energy greater than the activation energy, Ea, of the reaction, but they do not react. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: They collided with an orientation that did not bring the reacting atoms together.
items.misconception: No catalyst was present, and a reaction cannot take place at all without one.
items.why: Students meet catalysts mainly in industrial processes and enzymes in biology, where reactions are described as 'needing' a catalyst or enzyme; the idea of an extremely slow uncatalysed reaction is rarely shown. Collision theory explains any reaction without reference to a catalyst: collisions with E ≥ Ea and a proper orientation react. A catalyst increases the rate by providing an alternative pathway with a lower Ea; hydrogen peroxide, for example, decomposes slowly without a catalyst.
items.specStatementText: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
items.random_wrong: Their combined energy was less than the size of the enthalpy change of reaction, ΔH.

items.q: Two experiments use equal masses of calcium carbonate and the same volume of excess hydrochloric acid of the same concentration at the same temperature. In experiment 1 the calcium carbonate is a single lump; in experiment 2 it is a fine powder. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The powder reacts faster, as more of its particles are exposed, so collisions with acid are more frequent.
items.misconception: The lump reacts faster, as its greater size gives it the larger surface area for the acid particles to attack.
items.why: Students compare the surface of one piece with one piece, not the total surface of all the pieces, and link 'bigger' with 'more'. Compare equal masses. Each cut exposes new surface, so the powder has a much larger total surface area, more of its particles can be hit by the other reactant, collisions are more frequent, and it reacts faster.
items.specStatementText: Factors that influence the rate of a reaction include pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
items.random_wrong: The powder reacts faster, as its exposed particles collide with the acid particles with more energy.

items.q: Hydrogen iodide decomposes: 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g). A sample of hydrogen iodide is compressed to half its volume at constant temperature. What is the effect on the rate of reaction, and why?
items.correct: It increases: collisions become more frequent, and the fraction with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.
items.misconception: It is unchanged: there are equal amounts of gas on both sides of the equation, so pressure has no effect.
items.why: Students study rates and equilibrium together and apply the familiar equilibrium rule to both; conflating the two is widely reported in chemistry-education research. Treat kinetics with collision theory. For a gas, pressure changes the concentration of the reacting molecules, and so the collision frequency and the rate, regardless of how many gas molecules are on each side of the equation.
items.specStatementText: Factors that influence the rate of a reaction include pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
items.random_wrong: It increases: the compressed molecules collide more energetically, so more collisions exceed Ea.

items.q: A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is plotted for a sample of gas at 300 K, with number of particles on the y-axis and kinetic energy on the x-axis. The curve starts at the origin, rises to a peak and falls to a long tail that approaches the energy axis. Which describes the curve for the same sample at 400 K?
items.correct: The peak is lower and at a higher energy, the tail is higher, and the area under the curve is unchanged.
items.misconception: The peak is higher and at a higher energy, as more particles move fast, and the area is larger.
items.why: Students associate 'higher temperature' with 'more' and draw a bigger curve; they do not connect the area under the curve with the fixed number of particles. The number of particles in the sample does not change on heating, so the area under the curve is constant. Because the distribution spreads to higher energies, the curve must become flatter: the peak is lower and shifted to the right.
items.specStatementText: Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
items.random_wrong: The whole curve moves to higher energy by the same amount, keeping its shape and height.

items.q: For a reaction with Ea = 50 kJ mol⁻¹, raising the temperature from 300 K to 310 K almost doubles the rate. Which statement gives the main reason for this large increase?
items.correct: A much larger fraction of all the collisions now have energy equal to or greater than Ea.
items.misconception: The particles move faster, so they collide more often, and more collisions give more reactions.
items.why: Collision frequency is the first explanation students meet for concentration, pressure and surface area, and they extend it to every factor. The idea that heated particles 'move faster so collide more' is intuitive and often accepted in marking at pre-IB level. Distinguish two effects: how often particles collide, and what fraction of collisions succeed. Temperature mainly changes the fraction with E ≥ Ea (the area beyond Ea on the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve); a catalyst changes the fraction by lowering Ea.
items.specStatementText: Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
items.random_wrong: The activation energy decreases as the temperature rises, so more of the collisions succeed.

items.q: Catalase is an enzyme that catalyses the exothermic decomposition of hydrogen peroxide: 2H₂O₂(aq) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g). The energy profile of the uncatalysed reaction rises from the reactants to a maximum and falls to products that are lower in energy than the reactants. How does the profile differ when catalase is present?
items.correct: The maximum is lower, while the energies of the reactants and products, and so ΔH, are unchanged.
items.misconception: The maximum is lower and the products are lower in energy, so the reaction becomes more exothermic.
items.why: Students see a lower curve on the catalysed energy profile and assume the whole profile, including the products, is lowered; 'lowering the energy needed' is also confused with changing ΔH. The catalysed and uncatalysed profiles start at the same reactant energy and end at the same product energy; only the maximum (Ea) is lower. ΔH is the same.
items.specStatementText: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea.
items.random_wrong: The reactants are raised to a higher energy, closer to the top of an unchanged maximum.

items.q: A Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is drawn for a reaction mixture at constant temperature. The activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction is marked as a vertical line far out in the tail of the curve; the activation energy of the catalysed pathway is marked as a second vertical line at a lower energy. Which statement explains why the catalysed reaction is faster?
items.correct: The curve is unchanged, but a larger area lies beyond the lower Ea, so more collisions succeed.
items.misconception: The catalyst gives the particles extra energy, moving the curve to higher energies past the Ea line.
items.why: Students know that energy is needed to overcome Ea and assume that anything that helps must supply energy, as heating does; 'a catalyst helps particles over the barrier' encourages this. At a fixed temperature the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution is the same with or without a catalyst. What changes is the position of Ea: it is lower for the catalysed pathway, so a larger fraction of the same distribution lies beyond it.
items.specStatementText: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea.
items.random_wrong: The catalyst makes the particles collide more often, while the fraction with E ≥ Ea stays the same.

items.q: For a hypothetical endothermic reaction, the uncatalysed forward activation energy is 280 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔH = +110 kJ mol⁻¹. A catalyst lowers the forward activation energy to 230 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction?
items.correct: +120 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +170 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Reactions are usually written and discussed in the forward direction, and industrial catalysts are described as 'making more product', so students do not consider the reverse reaction. Both directions pass through the same transition state. Lowering that maximum lowers Ea(forward) and Ea(reverse) equally, and the difference between them, ΔH, is unchanged.

Working: On the energy profile the products lie 110 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants. The catalysed maximum lies 230 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants, so it lies 230 − 110 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹ above the products: Ea(reverse, catalysed) = +120 kJ mol⁻¹. Check: the catalyst lowers both barriers by the same 280 − 230 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹; the uncatalysed reverse Ea is 280 − 110 = 170 kJ mol⁻¹, and 170 − 50 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea.
items.random_wrong: −110 kJ mol⁻¹
items.working: On the energy profile the products lie 110 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants. The catalysed maximum lies 230 kJ mol⁻¹ above the reactants, so it lies 230 − 110 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹ above the products: Ea(reverse, catalysed) = +120 kJ mol⁻¹. Check: the catalyst lowers both barriers by the same 280 − 230 = 50 kJ mol⁻¹; the uncatalysed reverse Ea is 280 − 110 = 170 kJ mol⁻¹, and 170 − 50 = 120 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Nitrogen monoxide reacts with hydrogen: 2NO(g) + 2H₂(g) → N₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[NO]²[H₂]. Which proposed mechanism is consistent with both the rate equation and the overall equation?
items.correct: 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂O + H₂O (slow); N₂O + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O (fast)
items.misconception: 2NO → N₂O₂ (slow); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂; H₂O₂ + H₂ → 2H₂O (both fast)
items.why: Many textbook examples (such as the hydrolysis of a tertiary halogenoalkane) have a slow first step, and 'the reaction cannot go faster than its first step' sounds logical. Identify the slowest step, wherever it is. If a fast step comes first, its products feed the slow step, so the species from the fast step appear in the rate equation too.
items.specStatementText: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂ (fast); N₂O₂ + H₂ → N₂ + H₂O₂ (slow); H₂O₂ → 2OH (fast)

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a reaction intermediate from a transition state in a multistep reaction?
items.correct: An intermediate lies at an energy minimum between steps; a transition state is at a maximum and cannot be isolated.
items.misconception: A transition state can be isolated if the reaction is stopped quickly enough, just as an intermediate can.
items.why: Transition states are drawn with structural formulae in square brackets, just like real species, and both are described as 'formed during the reaction'. Look at the energy profile: an intermediate sits in a dip and so has a lifetime; a transition state sits at a peak and falls apart as soon as it forms.
items.specStatementText: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: An intermediate is present at the start and is re-formed at the end; a transition state is used up.

items.q: A reaction occurs in two steps. Its energy profile, with energies relative to the reactants, shows: reactants 0 kJ mol⁻¹; a first maximum at +45 kJ mol⁻¹; a minimum at +15 kJ mol⁻¹; a second maximum at +80 kJ mol⁻¹; products −20 kJ mol⁻¹. What is the activation energy of the rate-determining step?
items.correct: +65 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: +80 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
For a single-step reaction Ea is measured from the reactants, and students apply the same reading to every maximum on a multistep profile. For step 2, read the energy of the intermediate and subtract it from the energy of transition state 2. Each step starts from its own reactant species.

Working: Ea(step 1) = E(TS1) − E(reactants) = 45 − 0 = 45 kJ mol⁻¹. Ea(step 2) = E(TS2) − E(intermediate) = 80 − 15 = 65 kJ mol⁻¹. Step 2 has the larger Ea (and TS2 is the highest point), so step 2 is rate-determining: Ea = +65 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: Energy profiles can be used to show the activation energy and transition state of the rate-determining step in a multistep reaction.
items.random_wrong: +45 kJ mol⁻¹
items.working: Ea(step 1) = E(TS1) − E(reactants) = 45 − 0 = 45 kJ mol⁻¹. Ea(step 2) = E(TS2) − E(intermediate) = 80 − 15 = 65 kJ mol⁻¹. Step 2 has the larger Ea (and TS2 is the highest point), so step 2 is rate-determining: Ea = +65 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: Nitrogen dioxide reacts with carbon monoxide: NO₂(g) + CO(g) → NO(g) + CO₂(g), ΔH = −226 kJ mol⁻¹. The experimentally determined rate equation is rate = k[NO₂]². The proposed mechanism is step 1: 2NO₂(g) → NO₃(g) + NO(g); step 2: NO₃(g) + CO(g) → NO₂(g) + CO₂(g). Which statement about the energy profile for this mechanism follows from these data?
items.correct: The rise from the reactants to the first maximum exceeds that from the minimum to the second, as step 1 is slow.
items.misconception: The first maximum is the transition state of a unimolecular step, as only NO₂ reacts in step 1.
items.why: Students count the formulae written on the left-hand side rather than reading the coefficient, especially when a coefficient of 2 is in front of one species. Count every reacting particle, including those shown by a coefficient: 2NO₂ means two molecules. In a rate equation, likewise, the exponent (2 in [A]²), not the number of species, gives the order.
items.specStatementText: Energy profiles can be used to show the activation energy and transition state of the rate-determining step in a multistep reaction.
items.random_wrong: The first maximum is the highest point on the profile, as step 1 is the rate-determining step.

items.q: Which statement about molecularity is correct?
items.correct: 2NO₂(g) → NO₃(g) + NO(g) is a bimolecular step.
items.misconception: N₂O₄(g) → 2NO₂(g) is a termolecular step.
items.why: The term is learned as a label for a whole equation, and students count all the formulae in it. Count only the particles on the left-hand side of the elementary step. N₂O₄ → 2NO₂ involves one reacting particle, so it is unimolecular.
items.specStatementText: The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of reacting particles taking part in that step.
items.random_wrong: 2NO(g) → N₂O₂(g) is a unimolecular step.

items.q: A reaction has the overall equation 2A + B → C + D. A student states that its rate equation must be rate = k[A]²[B]. Which response is correct?
items.correct: The rate equation can only be found by experiment, and its orders need not match the coefficients.
items.misconception: The student is correct, as orders are the coefficients of the reactants in the balanced equation.
items.why: Writing an equilibrium expression from the balanced equation is a familiar procedure, and students assume the rate equation is written the same way. This is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in kinetics. Determine orders from data, for example by the initial rates method. The balanced equation shows the overall stoichiometry, not what collides in the rate-determining step.
items.specStatementText: Rate equations depend on the mechanism of the reaction and can only be determined experimentally.
items.random_wrong: The rate equation must include the products, written as rate = k[C][D]/[A]²[B], like K.

items.q: The initial rate of the reaction A + 2B → C was measured at constant temperature. Experiment 1: [A] = 0.010 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 2: [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 6.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. Experiment 3: [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, [B] = 0.060 mol dm⁻³, initial rate = 1.8 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the rate equation?
items.correct: rate = k[A]²[B]¹
items.misconception: rate = k[A]⁴[B]³
items.why:
When a concentration is doubled, first order doubles the rate, which makes 'order = factor' appear to work; students do not see that the relationship is an exponent. Use (factor change in concentration)^order = factor change in rate. Tripling [B] and tripling the rate gives 3^n = 3, so n = 1; doubling [A] and quadrupling the rate gives 2^n = 4, so n = 2.

Working: Exp 1 → 2: [A] × 2, [B] constant, rate × (6.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 4 = 2², so order in A = 2. Exp 2 → 3: [B] × 3, [A] constant, rate × (1.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(6.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 3 = 3¹, so order in B = 1. Rate = k[A]²[B]; overall order 3.
items.specStatementText: Rate equations depend on the mechanism of the reaction and can only be determined experimentally.
items.random_wrong: rate = k[A]¹[B]²
items.working: Exp 1 → 2: [A] × 2, [B] constant, rate × (6.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(1.5 × 10⁻⁵) = 4 = 2², so order in A = 2. Exp 2 → 3: [B] × 3, [A] constant, rate × (1.8 × 10⁻⁴)/(6.0 × 10⁻⁵) = 3 = 3¹, so order in B = 1. Rate = k[A]²[B]; overall order 3.

items.q: A reaction is zero order with respect to reactant X. Which statement about a graph for this reaction is correct?
items.correct: The concentration–time graph for X is a straight line with a negative gradient.
items.misconception: The concentration–time graph for X is a horizontal line, as X is not used up in the reaction.
items.why: Students read 'does not appear in the rate equation' as 'does not react', and a horizontal rate–concentration line as 'nothing is happening'. A zero-order reactant is consumed at a constant rate, so its concentration–time graph is a straight line with a negative gradient. It is in the overall equation, and usually reacts in a fast step after the rate-determining step.
items.specStatementText: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate-determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
items.random_wrong: The rate–concentration graph for X is a straight line sloping downwards, with a negative gradient.

items.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A][B]². At constant temperature, the concentrations of A and B are both doubled. By what factor does the rate increase?
items.why:
Students use additive rather than multiplicative reasoning in proportion problems, an error widely documented in mathematics and science education. For rate = k[A][B]², doubling both gives 2¹ × 2² = 8 times the rate, not 2 + 4 = 6.

Working: New rate/old rate = (2[A])(2[B])²/([A][B]²) = 2¹ × 2² = 8.
items.specStatementText: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate-determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.

items.q: Reactant A is used up in two separate reactions at constant temperature. Reaction 1 is first order with respect to A and reaction 2 is second order with respect to A. Which statement about graphs for these reactions is correct?
items.correct: For reaction 2, a graph of rate against [A] curves up from the origin, as doubling [A] quadruples the rate.
items.misconception: For reaction 2, a graph of rate against [A] is a straight line through the origin, as for reaction 1.
items.why: Direct proportionality is the relationship students meet most often in science, and 'more reactant, faster reaction' is taught before orders; over-use of linear reasoning is widely documented. Read the order from the rate equation or from data. For rate = k[A]², doubling [A] quadruples the rate; for rate = k[A]⁰ = k, changing [A] has no effect on the rate.
items.specStatementText: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate-determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
items.random_wrong: For reaction 1, a graph of rate against [A] is a curve that falls towards zero, like the [A]–time graph.

items.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]², with concentrations in mol dm⁻³ and the rate in mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What are the units of k?
items.correct: mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹, as k = rate/[A]² for a second-order reaction
items.misconception: mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹, as the rate constant has the same units as the rate
items.why: k is introduced as 'the rate constant', so students assume it measures the same thing as the rate. Derive the units: k = rate/[A]^m[B]^n. For a second-order reaction, (mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/(mol dm⁻³)² = mol⁻¹ dm³ s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The rate constant, k, is temperature dependent and its units are determined from the overall order of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: s⁻¹, as only one reactant, A, appears in the rate equation

items.q: The rate equation for a reaction is rate = k[A]²[B]. When [A] = 0.020 mol dm⁻³ and [B] = 0.050 mol dm⁻³, the rate is 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. What is the value of k?
items.correct: 1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
items.misconception: 1.5 × 10⁻² mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
items.why:
Confusing a power with multiplication by the index is a well-documented error in school algebra, and it gives the right answer for 2² = 2 × 2, which hides the mistake. Square the concentration: (0.020)² = 0.00040. Check that the powers are applied before multiplying the terms together.

Working: k = rate/([A]²[B]) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/((0.020 mol dm⁻³)² × 0.050 mol dm⁻³) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol³ dm⁻⁹) = 1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The rate constant, k, is temperature dependent and its units are determined from the overall order of the reaction.
items.random_wrong: 0.030 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹
items.working: k = rate/([A]²[B]) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹)/((0.020 mol dm⁻³)² × 0.050 mol dm⁻³) = (3.0 × 10⁻⁵)/(2.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol³ dm⁻⁹) = 1.5 mol⁻² dm⁶ s⁻¹.

items.q: The rate constant of a reaction varies with absolute temperature according to the Arrhenius equation, k = Ae^(−Ea/RT). A student plots ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis) for one reaction over a range of temperatures. Which describes the graph?
items.correct: A straight line with a negative gradient, equal to −Ea/R
items.misconception: A horizontal line, as k is a constant for a given reaction
items.why: The word 'constant' suggests a value that never changes, like R or N_A, and rate calculations are usually set at one temperature. k is constant with respect to concentration, not temperature. k = Ae^(−Ea/RT): as T rises, −Ea/RT becomes less negative and k increases.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius equation uses the temperature dependence of the rate constant to determine the activation energy.
items.random_wrong: A straight line with a negative gradient, equal to −Ea

items.q: A plot of ln k (y-axis) against 1/T (x-axis, in K⁻¹) for a reaction is a straight line with a gradient of −6.00 × 10³ K. Using ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the activation energy of the reaction?
items.correct: 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: 6.00 × 10³ J mol⁻¹
items.why:
Students remember that 'the gradient gives Ea' without the full relationship, and the R in the exponent is easily overlooked. Compare ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A with y = mx + c: m = −Ea/R. Multiply by R to obtain Ea.

Working: ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A has the form y = mx + c, so gradient = −Ea/R. Ea = −gradient × R = −(−6.00 × 10³ K) × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius equation uses the temperature dependence of the rate constant to determine the activation energy.
items.random_wrong: 0.722 kJ mol⁻¹
items.working: ln k = −(Ea/R)(1/T) + ln A has the form y = mx + c, so gradient = −Ea/R. Ea = −gradient × R = −(−6.00 × 10³ K) × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 4.99 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 49.9 kJ mol⁻¹.

items.q: The rate constant of a first-order reaction is 2.00 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 25.0 °C and 8.00 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ at 45.0 °C. Using ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the activation energy of the reaction?
items.correct: 54.6 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: 0.65 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
Temperatures are usually given in °C in experiments, and the conversion is forgotten when attention is on the logarithms. Convert every temperature to kelvin (T = θ + 273) before calculating 1/T. Using °C gives values of 1/T that are far too large and an Ea that is wrong by orders of magnitude.

Working: T₁ = 25.0 + 273 = 298 K; T₂ = 45.0 + 273 = 318 K. ln k₂ − ln k₁ = (Ea/R)(1/T₁ − 1/T₂). ln(8.00 × 10⁻³/2.00 × 10⁻³) = ln 4 = 1.386. 1/298 − 1/318 = 3.356 × 10⁻³ − 3.145 × 10⁻³ = 2.111 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹. Ea = R ln 4/(1/T₁ − 1/T₂) = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × 1.386/(2.111 × 10⁻⁴ K⁻¹) = 5.46 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 54.6 kJ mol⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.
items.random_wrong: 23.7 kJ mol⁻¹

items.q: A first-order reaction has Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹, and its rate constant at 127 °C is 3.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹. Using k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the Arrhenius factor, A?
items.why:
Ea is always quoted in kJ mol⁻¹ but R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, and students do not check that the units in Ea/RT cancel. Check that Ea/RT is dimensionless: J mol⁻¹ ÷ (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ × K). Convert kJ to J before substituting, and J to kJ at the end.

Working: T = 127 + 273 = 400 K; Ea = 100 kJ mol⁻¹ = 100 000 J mol⁻¹. Ea/RT = 100 000/(8.31 × 400) = 30.08. A = k/e^(−Ea/RT) = k × e^(Ea/RT) = 3.0 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹ × e^30.08 = 3.0 × 10⁻³ × 1.16 × 10¹³ = 3.5 × 10¹⁰ s⁻¹ (A has the same units as k). Equivalently ln A = ln k + Ea/RT = −5.81 + 30.08 = 24.27, and A = e^24.27.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.

items.q: Reaction 1 occurs between two gaseous atoms. Reaction 2 occurs between two large gaseous molecules and happens only if they collide at one particular site on each molecule. Assume the two reactions have the same Ea and the same collision frequency at a given temperature. Which reaction has the larger Arrhenius factor, A, and why?
items.correct: Reaction 1, as a greater fraction of its collisions have a suitable orientation for reaction.
items.misconception: Neither: A depends only on the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea, which is the same.
items.why: Both factors in k = Ae^(−Ea/RT) are linked to 'successful collisions', and students do not separate the energy condition from the orientation condition. Split the Arrhenius equation into its two conditions: e^(−Ea/RT) is the energy condition and A covers how often collisions occur with a proper orientation.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.
items.random_wrong: Neither: A depends only on how often the particles collide, which is the same for both.

items.q: A proposed mechanism for the reaction H₂(g) + I₂(g) → 2HI(g) is: step 1: I₂(g) ⇌ 2I(g) (fast); step 2: H₂(g) + 2I(g) → 2HI(g) (slow). Which statement about molecularity in this mechanism is correct?
items.correct: The slow step is termolecular, as one H₂ molecule and two I atoms must all collide together in it.
items.misconception: The overall reaction is bimolecular, as one H₂ molecule collides with one I₂ molecule.
items.why: Equations are written as a single event, and students read them as a picture of what happens rather than as a statement of amounts. A simultaneous collision of three or more particles is very unlikely. The overall equation is the sum of the elementary steps; the actual steps must be deduced from kinetic evidence.
items.specStatementText: The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of reacting particles taking part in that step.
items.random_wrong: Step 2 is bimolecular, as it involves two different reacting species, H₂ and I.

items.q: The graph shows Maxwell–Boltzmann energy distributions, P and Q, for the same sample of a gas at two different temperatures. The activation energy, Ea, of a reaction of the gas is marked. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Q is at the higher temperature, and more of its particles have energies of at least Ea.
items.misconception: Q is at the higher temperature, because every one of its particles has more energy than any particle in P.
items.why: Temperature is taught as a measure of particle energy, and statements such as 'particles move faster when heated' suggest that every particle speeds up by the same amount. At any temperature particles have a wide range of energies, and collisions constantly redistribute energy between them. At a higher temperature the Maxwell–Boltzmann curve is lower and broader with its peak at a higher energy; some particles still have low energies.
items.specStatementText: Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
items.random_wrong: P is at the higher temperature, because its higher peak shows more of its particles have energy above Ea.

figure.alt: Maxwell–Boltzmann graph: number of particles (vertical axis) against kinetic energy (horizontal axis), no numbers. Curve P rises steeply from the origin to a high, narrow peak at low energy and falls quickly. Curve Q rises more gradually to a lower, broader peak further along the energy axis and falls more slowly, so its tail lies above P's at high energies; the two curves cross once. A vertical dashed line labelled Ea is drawn far to the right of both peaks, in the tail region.

items.q: The diagram shows the energy profile of an exothermic reaction without a catalyst (solid line) and with a catalyst (dashed line). Which arrow represents the activation energy of the catalysed reverse reaction?
items.correct: Arrow Z
items.misconception: Arrow X
items.why: Both quantities appear on the same energy profile and both are 'energy for the reaction' in kJ mol⁻¹, so students confuse thermodynamic and kinetic quantities. The confusion between Ea and ΔH, and the belief that more exothermic reactions are faster, are both widely reported. On an energy profile Ea is measured from the reactants up to the maximum, and ΔH from the reactants to the products. A strongly exothermic reaction can be very slow if Ea is large.
items.specStatementText: Catalysts increase the rate of reaction by providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower Ea.
items.random_wrong: Arrow Y

items.q: The graph shows how the concentration of a reactant, A, changes with time at constant temperature. A tangent to the curve has been drawn at t = 100 s. What is the rate of reaction at t = 100 s?
items.correct: 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.misconception: 4.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹
items.why:
Rates are first met as average rates (a change divided by the time taken), and students carry this calculation over to the rate at an instant; pre-IB courses rarely separate an average rate from an instantaneous one. Draw a tangent to the curve at that moment and find its gradient. A chord from the start to that moment gives only the average rate over that interval.

Working: The rate at 100 s is the gradient of the tangent at that point. The tangent crosses the [A] axis at 0.090 mol dm⁻³ and the time axis at 300 s, so gradient = (0.000 − 0.090) mol dm⁻³ ÷ (300 − 0) s = −3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The rate is quoted as a positive value for the decrease in [A]: rate = 3.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
items.random_wrong: 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

items.q: The graph shows the volume of hydrogen collected against time when the same mass of magnesium ribbon reacts with an excess of hydrochloric acid in two experiments, P and Q. One experiment used 1.0 mol dm⁻³ acid and the other 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid; all other conditions were identical. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Q used the 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid, since more frequent collisions give it the steeper curve and higher rate.
items.misconception: The rates of P and Q are the same, since both experiments produce the same final volume of hydrogen.
items.why: Students conflate 'how fast' with 'how much', a confusion widely reported in chemistry-education research on kinetics; in everyday life doing something faster often means getting more done. The rate is the change in concentration per unit time. With the same amounts of reactants, a faster reaction gives the same total amount of product; its graph simply levels off sooner at the same final value.
items.specStatementText: Factors that influence the rate of a reaction include pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
items.random_wrong: P used the 2.0 mol dm⁻³ acid, since its reaction continues for longer and so has the higher rate.

figure.alt: Graph of volume of hydrogen (vertical axis) against time (horizontal axis), no numbers. Two curves start at the origin. Curve Q rises steeply and levels off early at a constant final volume. Curve P rises less steeply, taking much longer to level off, but reaches exactly the same final volume as Q.

items.q: The graph shows how the initial rate of the reaction A + B → C varies with the initial concentration of A, with [B] and the temperature kept constant. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The order with respect to A is zero, so [A] does not appear in the rate equation, although A is consumed.
items.misconception: A graph of [A] against time for this reaction would also be a horizontal line, as the rate does not depend on [A].
items.why: Six graph shapes are learned together, and students remember 'straight line' or 'curve' for an order without attaching it to the right axes. Work from the rate equation. On a rate–concentration graph, zero order gives rate = k (horizontal), first order gives rate = k[X] (straight line through the origin). On a concentration–time graph, a constant rate gives a straight line with a negative gradient.
items.specStatementText: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate-determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
items.random_wrong: A takes no part in the reaction, since changing its concentration has no effect on the rate.

items.q: The graph shows how the concentration of A changes with time for the reaction 2A(g) → B(g) + C(g) at constant temperature. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The reaction is first order with respect to A, as [A] halves in equal time intervals.
items.misconception: The reaction is second order with respect to A, as the coefficient of A in the equation is 2.
items.why: Writing an equilibrium expression from the balanced equation is a familiar procedure, and students assume the rate equation is written the same way. This is one of the most widely reported misconceptions in kinetics. Determine orders from data, for example by the initial rates method. The balanced equation shows the overall stoichiometry, not what collides in the rate-determining step.
items.specStatementText: The order of a reaction with respect to a reactant is the exponent to which the concentration of the reactant is raised in the rate equation. The order with respect to a reactant can describe the number of particles taking part in the rate-determining step. The overall reaction order is the sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
items.random_wrong: The reaction is zero order with respect to A, as A is being used up at one steady rate.

items.q: The graph shows ln k plotted against 1/T for a reaction; two points on the line are marked. Using ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A and R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the activation energy of the reaction?
items.correct: 66 kJ mol⁻¹
items.misconception: 0.96 kJ mol⁻¹
items.why:
A rearrangement error: seeing R in the expression −Ea/R, students divide by R again instead of multiplying both sides by R to isolate Ea. Isolate Ea step by step: gradient = −Ea/R, so multiply both sides by R and change the sign, Ea = −gradient × R. A unit check helps: K × J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ gives J mol⁻¹, whereas K ÷ J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ does not give an energy unit.

Working: Reading the marked points: (1/T = 2.5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −2.0) and (1/T = 3.5 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, ln k = −10.0). Gradient = Δ(ln k)/Δ(1/T) = (−10.0 − (−2.0)) ÷ ((3.5 − 2.5) × 10⁻³ K⁻¹) = −8.0 ÷ 1.0 × 10⁻³ = −8.0 × 10³ K. Since gradient = −Ea/R, Ea = −gradient × R = 8.0 × 10³ K × 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ = 6.65 × 10⁴ J mol⁻¹ = 66 kJ mol⁻¹ (2 s.f.).
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius equation uses the temperature dependence of the rate constant to determine the activation energy.
items.random_wrong: 8.0 kJ mol⁻¹

items.q: The diagram shows the energy profile of a reaction that occurs in two elementary steps. Which arrow represents the activation energy of the rate-determining step?
items.correct: Arrow X
items.misconception: Arrow W
items.why: Many textbook examples (such as the hydrolysis of a tertiary halogenoalkane) have a slow first step, and 'the reaction cannot go faster than its first step' sounds logical. Identify the slowest step, wherever it is. If a fast step comes first, its products feed the slow step, so the species from the fast step appear in the rate equation too.
items.specStatementText: Energy profiles can be used to show the activation energy and transition state of the rate-determining step in a multistep reaction.

items.q: When calculating the gradient of a tangent, which quantity goes on top?
items.correct: The change in the quantity on the y-axis (concentration, volume or mass) divided by the change in time on the x-axis.
items.misconception: The gradient of a tangent is the change in the x-axis quantity divided by the change in the y-axis quantity.
items.why: Confusing 'rise over run' with 'run over rise' is a common error in graph work generally, especially when students calculate gradients mechanically without checking units. Gradient = Δy/Δx. For a volume–time graph this is Δ(volume)/Δ(time), in cm³ s⁻¹. Checking the units catches the error: Δt/ΔV would have units of s cm⁻³, which is not a rate.
items.specStatementText: The rate of reaction is expressed as the change in concentration of a particular reactant/product per unit time.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is enough energy all that a collision needs for reaction?
items.correct: No. A collision must also have a proper orientation, so that the atoms that form the new bonds meet.
items.misconception: Whether a collision leads to reaction depends only on how much energy it has (or simply on how often particles collide); the orientation of the particles does not matter.
items.why: Particle diagrams at GCSE show molecules as simple spheres, for which orientation has no meaning, and energy is the only criterion students meet in early treatments of collision theory. Collision theory has two conditions: energy equal to or greater than Ea, and a proper orientation (collision geometry). Many collisions with enough energy fail because the reacting atoms do not meet.
items.specStatementText: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does raising the temperature lower the activation energy?
items.correct: No. Ea is a property of the reaction pathway and is unchanged by temperature. Raising the temperature increases the fraction of particles with energy equal to or greater than the same Ea.
items.misconception: Heating lowers the activation energy, so more collisions have enough energy to react.
items.why: Both heating and catalysts make reactions faster, and students merge the two explanations; 'heat helps the reaction get over the barrier' is misread as 'heat lowers the barrier'. This belief is widely reported in chemistry-education research on kinetics. Only a change of pathway (for example a catalyst) changes Ea. On a Maxwell–Boltzmann diagram the Ea line stays where it is when the temperature rises; the curve changes so that a larger area lies beyond it.
items.specStatementText: Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the mean kinetic energy of the particles depend on how much of the substance there is?
items.correct: No. The mean kinetic energy per particle depends only on the absolute temperature. A larger sample has more total energy, but not more energy per particle.
items.misconception: The kinetic energy of the particles depends on how much of the substance there is: a larger sample holds more heat, so its particles have more kinetic energy.
items.why: In everyday language 'heat' and 'temperature' are used interchangeably; confusion between them is one of the most widely documented misconceptions in science education. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy per particle; the total thermal energy of a sample depends on both its temperature and how many particles it contains. Two samples at the same temperature have the same mean kinetic energy per particle whatever their sizes.
items.specStatementText: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the activation energy a one-off input of energy that starts a reaction?
items.correct: No. Ea is the minimum energy that each colliding pair of particles needs for that collision to react. A spark or heating only gives some particles enough energy; every successful collision must itself have E ≥ Ea and a proper orientation.
items.misconception: Activation energy is a one-off input of energy, such as a spark or a flame, needed to start a reaction off; without that outside input no collision can react, whatever its energy.
items.why: Pre-IB definitions often describe Ea as 'the energy needed to start a reaction', and demonstrations such as lighting a Bunsen burner or igniting hydrogen show a reaction that needs a flame or spark only at the start. Ea applies to every collision, not to the reaction as a whole. A flame starts a combustion because it gives some molecules energy ≥ Ea; the energy released then keeps enough later collisions above Ea. A collision that already has E ≥ Ea needs no outside energy.
items.specStatementText: Activation energy, Ea, is the minimum energy that colliding particles need for a successful collision leading to a reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does increasing concentration, pressure or surface area make each collision more energetic?
items.correct: No. These changes make collisions more frequent. The energy of each collision depends on temperature, so the fraction of collisions with E ≥ Ea is unchanged.
items.misconception: Crowding the particles together, or breaking up a solid, makes the particles collide harder, so a larger fraction of collisions have enough energy to react.
items.why: Students picture 'more crowded' or 'squeezed' particles hitting each other harder, and blend the frequency explanation with the energy explanation for temperature. Only temperature changes the distribution of particle energies. Concentration, pressure and surface area change how often particles collide: more collisions per second, the same fraction successful, so more successful collisions per second.
items.specStatementText: Factors that influence the rate of a reaction include pressure, concentration, surface area, temperature and the presence of a catalyst.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a mechanism acceptable if it fits the rate equation, even if its steps do not add up to the overall equation?
items.correct: No. A mechanism must be consistent with both the kinetic data (the rate equation) and the stoichiometric data (the steps must add up to the overall equation).
items.misconception: A proposed mechanism only has to give the correct rate equation; it does not matter whether the steps add up to the overall equation.
items.why: Mechanism questions usually focus on matching the rate-determining step to the rate equation, so students check only that condition. Check a mechanism twice: add the steps and cancel intermediates to recover the overall equation; then check that the slow step, with any steps before it, gives the experimental rate equation.
items.specStatementText: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is an intermediate the same kind of species as a catalyst?
items.correct: No. An intermediate is formed in one step and used up in a later step. A catalyst is present at the start, is used in an early step and is re-formed in a later step.
items.misconception: An intermediate is present at the start of the reaction and is re-formed at the end, like a catalyst.
items.why: Both intermediates and catalysts cancel when the steps of a mechanism are added, so students do not distinguish them. Check the order in which a species appears: if it is first produced and then consumed, it is an intermediate; if it is first consumed and then regenerated, it is a catalyst.
items.specStatementText: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do intermediates appear in the overall equation?
items.correct: No. An intermediate is produced in one step and consumed in a later one, so it cancels when the steps are added and does not appear in the overall equation.
items.misconception: Intermediates are among the reactants or products in the overall equation for the reaction.
items.why: When adding the steps of a mechanism, students sometimes forget to cancel species that appear on both sides. Add the elementary steps and cancel every species that appears on both sides. The species that cancel (other than a catalyst) are the intermediates.
items.specStatementText: Many reactions occur in a series of elementary steps. The slowest step determines the rate of the reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a rate equation written like an equilibrium constant expression?
items.correct: No. A rate equation contains the concentrations of the species in the rate-determining step (and steps before it), raised to experimentally determined orders; products do not normally appear, and there is no 'products over reactants' form.
items.misconception: A rate equation is written like the expression for K, with the concentrations of the products divided by those of the reactants.
items.why: Both expressions use square brackets and a constant (k or K), and they are often taught close together. K is a ratio of equilibrium concentrations; the rate equation describes how fast the forward reaction goes. rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, with m and n found by experiment.
items.specStatementText: Rate equations depend on the mechanism of the reaction and can only be determined experimentally.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: How is k found from the rate equation (or A from the Arrhenius equation)?
items.correct: By dividing: k = rate/([A]^m[B]^n), and A = k/e^(−Ea/RT) = k × e^(Ea/RT).
items.misconception: To isolate k (or A), the other side of the equation is multiplied by the remaining terms rather than divided by them.
items.why: Rearranging equations with several multiplied terms is a common source of procedural error in chemistry calculations, particularly under time pressure. Whatever multiplies k on one side must divide the other side. Check with units: rate × [A]² has units mol³ dm⁻⁹ s⁻¹, which cannot be the units of a second-order rate constant.
items.specStatementText: The rate constant, k, is temperature dependent and its units are determined from the overall order of the reaction.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a graph of ln k against 1/T slope upwards because k increases with temperature?
items.correct: No. As T increases, 1/T decreases, so higher values of ln k are found at smaller values of 1/T and the line has a negative gradient, −Ea/R.
items.misconception: Because k increases with temperature, a graph of ln k against 1/T slopes upwards with a positive gradient.
items.why: Students carry the trend 'k rises with T' across to the graph without noticing that the x-axis is 1/T, not T. Plot a few points: high T means small 1/T and large ln k, so the line falls from left to right. Its gradient is −Ea/R.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius equation uses the temperature dependence of the rate constant to determine the activation energy.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can log₁₀ be used in place of ln in the Arrhenius equation?
items.correct: No. The linear form uses natural logarithms: ln k = −Ea/RT + ln A. Using log₁₀ without the conversion factor (ln x = 2.303 log₁₀ x) gives wrong values of Ea and A.
items.misconception: log₁₀ and ln are interchangeable in the Arrhenius equation, so either logarithm key on a calculator can be used.
items.why: Calculators have adjacent 'log' and 'ln' keys, and pH calculations have made log₁₀ the more familiar logarithm in chemistry. Use ln (natural logarithm) throughout, and e^x to reverse it. log₁₀ values are smaller by a factor of 2.303, so they give an Ea that is too small by that factor.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do heavier particles have more kinetic energy than lighter ones at the same temperature?
items.correct: No. At the same temperature all particles have the same mean kinetic energy; heavier particles move more slowly on average.
items.misconception: Heavier particles have more kinetic energy than lighter particles at the same temperature, because kinetic energy increases with mass.
items.why: Students apply E_k = ½mv² with the speed held fixed, and associate 'heavier' with 'more energy' as for everyday moving objects. The mean kinetic energy depends only on the absolute temperature. Because E_k = ½mv², a heavier particle with the same mean kinetic energy has a lower mean speed.
items.specStatementText: Species react as a result of collisions of sufficient energy and proper orientation.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Arrhenius factor, A, larger for a reaction that needs a particular collision orientation?
items.correct: No. A takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations. The stricter the orientation requirement, the smaller the fraction of collisions that are properly oriented, so the smaller A is.
items.misconception: Because A 'takes orientation into account', it is larger for a reaction whose particles must collide in a particular orientation.
items.why: A misreading of the definition: the guide says A 'takes into account' orientation, and students read this as a correction term that grows as the orientation requirement becomes stricter, without reasoning through the direction of the effect. A counts properly oriented collisions per unit time. The more orientations that fail, the fewer collisions count and the smaller A is; atoms, which react whatever their orientation, have the largest A for a given collision frequency.
items.specStatementText: The Arrhenius factor, A, takes into account the frequency of collisions with proper orientations.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the activation energy of the reverse reaction always the forward activation energy plus the size of ΔH?
items.correct: No. Ea(reverse) = Ea(forward) − ΔH. For an exothermic reaction (ΔH negative) the reverse barrier is larger than the forward one; for an endothermic reaction (ΔH positive) it is smaller.
items.misconception: The activation energy of the reverse reaction is found by adding the size of ΔH to the forward activation energy, whatever the sign of ΔH, as though the products always lay below the reactants.
items.why: Most energy profiles students meet are for exothermic reactions such as combustion and neutralization, where the reverse barrier is the forward barrier plus the size of ΔH; the rule is then applied to an endothermic profile without checking whether the products lie above or below the reactants. Read the reverse activation energy from the profile: it is the rise from the products up to the maximum. For an endothermic reaction the products lie above the reactants, so this rise is Ea(forward) − ΔH, which is smaller than Ea(forward).

items.q: On an Arrhenius plot the horizontal axis is labelled 1/T / 10⁻³ K⁻¹ and marked 2.5, 3.0 and 3.5. What value of 1/T does the mark 3.0 represent?
items.correct: 3.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹. The label means the plotted numbers are 1/T divided by 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so each reading must be multiplied by 10⁻³ to recover 1/T in K⁻¹.
items.misconception: The power of ten in an axis label such as 1/T / 10⁻³ K⁻¹ can be ignored, so the numbers printed on the axis are used as they stand when a gradient is calculated.
items.why: Students are used to axis labels that are just a quantity and a unit; a scale factor written into the label is easily overlooked, and the plotted numbers are typed straight into the calculator. Widely reported in examiner comments on graph-reading questions. A label of the form quantity / (factor × unit) means the plotted numbers equal the quantity divided by that factor and unit. Multiply each reading by the factor before using it: a change read as 1.0 on an axis in 10⁻³ K⁻¹ is 1.0 × 10⁻³ K⁻¹, so a gradient of −8.0 per axis unit is −8.0 × 10³ K.
